name: NanoLog (PlatformLab)
baseline: spdlog v1.1.0, glog v0.3.5 (also Log4j2, Boost.Log, ETW)
workload: Runtime latency (50th/99.9th percentile ns) of printf-style log calls, six message types, plus max throughput with 1-16 threads
claimed_speedup: Median 7-8 ns vs spdlog 214-1776 ns and glog 1198-2569 ns (README table); over 80 million logs/second
tradeoffs: Binary log output needs a separate decompressor to get text; preprocessor version needs a Python step in the build and produces a non-portable per-application library; C++17 version is closer to a regular library.
caveats: README table has no compiler flags or CPU model on the page (paper PDF at usenix.org was blocked here, so hardware not confirmed); spdlog v1.1.0 and glog v0.3.5 are old versions. NanoLog is not a text logger so throughput is not like-for-like. Independently re-measured in the Quill benchmark at 8 ns median vs spdlog 271 ns.
found_via: WebSearch: 'NanoLog nanosecond scale logging system github PlatformLab'; README Performance section

name: Quill
baseline: spdlog, g3log, Boost.Log (also fmtlog, XTR, NanoLog, BinLog, Reckless, BqLog as peers)
workload: Frontend latency of LOG_INFO with 3 numeric args, large strings and complex types, 1 and 4 threads, percentiles in ns
claimed_speedup: 1 thread logging numbers: 50th percentile 6 ns vs spdlog 271 ns and g3log 1066 ns; 4 threads 8 ns vs spdlog 557 ns
hardware: Intel Core i5-12600 @ 4.8 GHz, RHEL 9.4, benchmark-tuned (isolcpus, mitigations=off)
stars_or_usage: 3.0k stars; packaged in vcpkg, Conan, Homebrew
tradeoffs: Formatting happens on a backend thread; per-thread SPSC queues use memory per thread; bounded dropping queue may drop messages under load; async crash safety needs care.
caveats: Own benchmark (code at odygrd/logger_benchmarks, not opened); no glog or OpenTelemetry row in this table. BqLog's own benchmark claims 7-18x over Quill on a different machine.
found_via: WebSearch: 'quill C++ asynchronous low latency logging library benchmark spdlog'; README Performance section

name: fmtlog
workload: Front-end latency and throughput of six log message types using NanoLog's message map and spdlog's default header pattern
claimed_speedup: README (Xeon Gold 6144): ~6.4 ns latency vs spdlog 156-391 ns; throughput 2.95-7.08 M/s vs spdlog 2.56-6.37 M/s. In Quill benchmark, 1 thread 50th percentile 6 ns vs spdlog 271 ns
compiler_and_flags: Quill benchmark: GCC 14.2, -march=x86-64-v3. Own README: GCC 10.2 tested, flags not stated
hardware: Quill benchmark: Intel Core i5-12600. Own README: Intel Xeon Gold 6144 @ 3.50GHz
tradeoffs: Needs fmtlib and C++17; asynchronous, call fmtlog::poll() or run a polling thread; default queue 1 MB per thread and drops messages when full unless FMTLOG_BLOCK=1; static info table costs ~50 bytes per log statement.
caveats: Tier A rests on the Quill project's benchmark repo, which compares fmtlog against spdlog; fmtlog's own README table is first-party and states no flags. NanoLog throughput in the README is not comparable (binary output). No glog or OpenTelemetry comparison.
found_via: WebSearch: 'fmtlog fast logging library faster than spdlog github'; README Performance section and Quill README table

name: XTR
workload: Call-site latency of logging with 3 numeric args, large strings; own Google Benchmark of per-statement cost
claimed_speedup: Quill benchmark 1 thread 50th percentile 6 ns vs spdlog 271 ns; own README: 0.9-8.8 ns per call on Ryzen 5950X
compiler_and_flags: Quill benchmark: GCC 14.2, -march=x86-64-v3. Own README: g++ 15.3.0 lto-release
hardware: Quill benchmark: Intel Core i5-12600. Own README: Ryzen 5950X, SMT off, isolated cores
tradeoffs: Linux and FreeBSD x86-64 only; no allocations or system calls on log path; background thread optional; sanitizes non-printable characters.
caveats: Own README numbers are per-call microbenchmarks with no baseline row (README itself notes CPU scaling was on); the win over spdlog comes from the Quill project's benchmark table, where XTR is a peer entry. No glog or OpenTelemetry comparison.
found_via: Quill README performance table; WebSearch results listing XTR as alternative

name: BinLog (Morgan Stanley)
workload: Producer-side latency of structured binary log events (timestamped, async single-consumer queue)
claimed_speedup: Quill benchmark 1 thread 50th percentile 18 ns vs spdlog 271 ns; 4 threads 29 ns vs 557 ns. Own README: 8-38 ns median per event on Google Benchmark
stars_or_usage: 796 stars; repository archived by owner on 2026-07-01
tradeoffs: Produces binary structured logs needing bread/binlog tools to read as text; archived and read-only.
caveats: Own README benchmark names no baseline; the spdlog comparison is from the Quill benchmark. Archived, so no further fixes. 99.9th percentile tails reach 119-445 ns.
found_via: WebSearch: 'binary logging library C++ binlog benchmark faster than spdlog'; Quill README table

name: BqLog (Tencent)
workload: 1-10 threads each writing 2,000,000 log entries (4-parameter formatted and plain text), total time including flush to disk
claimed_speedup: Compressed mode 6-65x faster than spdlog (async) and 47-252x faster than glog; 7-16x faster than fmtlog, 7-18x than quill
stars_or_usage: 645 stars; used in Honor of Kings
tradeoffs: Compressed binary format needs a decoder tool; multi-language (Java, C#, Go, Python); crash recovery and encryption options.
caveats: First-party benchmark; runnable project at tag benchmark_2.5.0 (not opened). Contradicted in part by the Quill benchmark (Linux, GCC), where BqLog is 125 ns median vs fmtlog/Quill 6 ns and about 2x faster than spdlog (271 ns); glog baseline is synchronous. Benchmarks measure total time to flush, not call-site latency.
found_via: WebSearch: 'BqLog Tencent high performance logging benchmark spdlog log4j'; BENCHMARK.md
